'''William Edward Spicer''' (September 7, 1929 – June 6, 2004) was an American engineering academic.

Born in [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana]] on September 7, 1929, Spicer enrolled at the [[College of William and Mary]], earning his first bachelor's degree in physics in 1949, followed by an equivalent degree at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1951. He then attended [[University of Missouri]], completing master's and doctoral degrees in the same subject in 1953 and 1955, respectively. Spicer then worked for the [[Radio Corporation of America]] until 1962, when he joined the [[Stanford University]] faculty. Spicer received a [[Guggenheim fellowship]] in 1978, the same year he was appointed Stanford W. Ascherman Professor of Engineering. Spicer was granted emeritus status in 1992, and continued research work until his death of heart failure in London on June 6, 2004.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Levy |first1=Dawn |title=William Spicer, emeritus professor of engineering, dies at 74 |url=https://news.stanford.edu/news/2004/july7/spicerobit-77.html |accessdate=December 18, 2018 |publisher=Stanford University |date=June 1, 2004}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=W. E. Spicer |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11609030.html |accessdate=December 18, 2018 |publisher=American Institute of Physics}}</ref> Over the course of his career Spicer was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and the [[IEEE]], as well as member of the [[ American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. He was a co-recipient of the APS [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] in 1980, won the [[Medard W. Welch Award]] of the [[American Vacuum Society]] in 1984, followed by the Lifetime Mentor Award bestowed by AAAS in 2000.<ref>{{cite news |title=Memorial Resolution: William Edward Spicer |url=https://news.stanford.edu/news/2006/july12/memlspi-071206.html |accessdate=December 18, 2018 |publisher=Stanford University |date=July 12, 2006}}</ref>

After his death the Best Student Paper Award of the U.S. Workshop on the Physics and Chemistry of II-VI Materials was named for Spicer. Upon Thomas Noel Castleman's death in 2010,<ref>{{cite news |title=Thomas N. Casselman Obituary |url=http://obits.oregonlive.com/obituaries/oregon/obituary-preview.aspx?n=thomas-n-casselman&pid=145197707 |accessdate=December 18, 2018 |work=The Oregonian |date=September 9, 2010}}</ref> the award became known as the William E. Spicer - Thomas N. Casselman Award for Best Student Paper.<ref>{{cite news |title=William E. Spicer - Thomas N. Casselman Award |url=http://www.ii-viworkshop.org/spicer-casselman-award.php |accessdate=December 18, 2018 |publisher=U.S. Workshop on the Physics and Chemistry of II-VI Materials}}</ref>
